title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky criticises 'gift to Putin'
description: US President Donald Trump says he has reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Moscow to "immediately release" diesel to th
body: US President Donald Trump says he has reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Moscow to "immediately release" diesel to the US and globally. Trump said the proposed release of hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Russian diesel, in tranches, would see prices "COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!".It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April 2027 as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen. Ukraine's president criticised the decision, saying any easing of sanctions on Russia played into Moscow's hands and would prolong the war between the two countries.Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.He added that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period" after, dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have seen attacks by Ukraine.Putin later said Russia was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts.The BBC has asked the White House for clarity on what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment.Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US, as he has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which began in February, and its impact on global energy prices.That conflict has sent the cost of petrol and, in particular diesel, skyrocketing in America in recent months, which has soured his standing with the public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation.The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market. Putin said in a statement that he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large."An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."But Zelensky hit out at it, saying "gifts to Putin will not work for peace" and that Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror"."Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on social media.Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, and introduced a ban on diesel exports. According to the International Energy Agency, its diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%.Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.But Zelensky defended the strikes on Friday, saying there were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector"."Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information and the details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return is unclear. But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US, that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine.What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel.With the looming US midterm congressional elections - which will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain.Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax.Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns, and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

title: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
description: Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legi
body: Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear. It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy"."Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked."Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

schema.headline: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices

title: Three men found guilty of murdering two Australian surfer brothers and US friend
description: Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in
body: Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024.The men's full names could not be given for legal reasons, and they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús. They are yet to be sentenced - but are likely to spend the rest of their lives in a prison.Debra Robinson, the brother's mother, told the courtroom in the northern Baja California state the murders of her sons had taken "the future we had imagined with them".During the trial the court heard the tourists were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck in a secluded beach area. Their bodies were later found with gunshot wounds to their heads, dumped down a well.The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the coastal area is usually safe from the violence in other parts of Mexico.Debra Robinson and her husband Martin Robinson have been at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial and they delivered emotional testimony during closing arguments before Friday's verdict."It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," said Martin. Family members of Rhoad joined the trial by video link.Speaking to media outside court a week ago, Debra Robinson said the couple were "deeply grateful" to Australians for the outpouring of support they had received and that they "feel the love and their arms around us".During the month-long trial, the prosecution had sought 150 years in prison for each of the three defendants.In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo alias "El Kekas", was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.The beach town has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers and the chilling murders revealed much about how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.The only explanation the authorities appeared able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.Their killings took place barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week when their families were able to identify them.At the time, the surfer community in Ensenada turned out in force to commemorate the men by paddling out at one of the area's best known surfing spots and throwing flowers into the sea.Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.Amid the demands for action, Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila tried to ease public fears about the widespread violence in her state."Baja California is and will continue to be a state with safe tourism for the thousands of people who visit us from the rest of the country and the world", she said. "I send my condolences and solidarity to the families at this difficult time."

schema.headline: Three men found guilty of murdering two Australian surfer brothers and US friend

title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
description: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "di
body: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially.However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims.The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel.The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software.Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution.He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution.The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function.Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty".The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred".It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment."This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself.The sanctions could ultimately see the ICC unable to try cases, meaning detainees awaiting trial or judgment could have to be released, according to Professor Ryan Goodman from the New York University School of Law.Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines.The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Others awaiting trial or with pending appeals include former senior figures accused of war crimes in Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic.Goodman says that as a senator, Rubio was "out front" highlighting Duterte's alleged crimes.He told the BBC such a release would be "enormously damaging to the global effort towards international justice [and] towards the Philippines"."[For] the victims, it just has to be incredibly traumatic because a lot of them participate in the ICC proceedings to put themselves on the line with a hope that justice will come around," adds Goodman, a former special counsel at the US Department of Defence.Among the carve-outs announced as part of today's sanctions are "licenses" allowing the ICC to continue "services for the operation of facilities used for the detention" of Duterte and others.However, Goodman says ultimately these detainees may have to be released "as a matter of law" if the financial sanctions mean the court cannot conduct fair trials or appeals.

schema.headline: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'

title: Zack Polanski vows to stay as Green leader as he faces criticism after by-election defeat
description: Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Green Party leader after his by-election defeat, as he faced pressure from within his own party to resign.The le
body: Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Green Party leader after his by-election defeat, as he faced pressure from within his own party to resign.The leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, said on Friday he should resign, adding it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.Lichtenstein's comments come after two former Green leaders accused Polanski of failing to show leadership over the Zionism row.Polanski, who came second to Labour overnight in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and he "of course" had not questioned that.The Greens had hoped to take the seat, previously held by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, after a by-election success earlier this year.Polanski lost out in Thursday's contest in London to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali - who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22 percentage points on the 2024 general election.Following the by-election, Lichtenstein was asked whether it would be right for Polanski to continue as leader of the party. She told Times Radio: "No, I think he should resign."Earlier in the week, Lichtenstein, who has been a member of the Green Party for nearly three decades, told Radio 4's Today programme it was "quite possible" she would leave the party after the Zionism row. Speaking to the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire on Friday, she said she should would not resign immediately because she is having conversations about how to "detoxify" the party. When asked if she had confidence in Polanski's leadership, Lichtenstein said: "At the moment, no I don't." She added that she was "very disappointed" in him.Calling on Polanski to apologise, she said: "I don't think that any Jew in the party is going to be in any danger... "There just might be some unpleasant people who will direct some unpleasant comments, and some of us are going to have to deal with them robustly."Her criticisms were similar to those of former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas who said Polanski should have attended the vote on the conference motion on Sunday.The motion, which was passed by rank-and-file members to become official party policy, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.Adrian Ramsay, a Green MP and former co-leader, declined to back Polanski on Friday, and said he was now working to reverse the motion. "A lot depends on what happens in the days and weeks to come," he told the BBC's Politics East, when asked if Polanski should still lead the party."[He] did not show leadership I would have been looking for." Ellie Chowns, the Green MP for North Herefordshire, said she "unequivocally" backs Israel's right to exist and is "passionately opposed to the actions of the current Israeli government under Netanyahu"."I believe it's for both Israelis and Palestinians themselves to decide what the ultimate constitutional settlement should look like in their region," she told BBC News."I believe both Israel and Palestine have the right to exist."I believe that's a perspective shared by the large majority of Green Party members and by the large majority of the British people."Polanski defended his absence from the controversial motion vote in Brighton, saying he was busy campaigning in the North London constituency.Asked if he would resign, he said: "Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green Party."Yes, I've taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion."Having not answered questions about the Zionism vote for most of this week, Polanski confirmed in interviews on Friday that he would not have voted for the "imperfect" motion without it being amended.However, he said "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology".Several UN reports have accused the Israeli government of committing war crimes which amount to genocide in Gaza. Israel has repeatedly denied all such allegations.On Friday morning, following the Zionism row, Polanski was asked repeatedly on BBC Radio 4's Today programme whether he believes Israel has a right to exist."I don't believe any state has the right to oppress or to commit apartheid and certainly not genocide on another people," he said, adding: "I don't believe that's a state that anyone should be supporting."Asked by presenter Nick Robinson for a "yes/no" answer on this question, he said: "I've repeated many times that I want to see equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - at the moment Palestinians don't have equal rights so I think I'm answering your question really clearly."But given his popularity among the grassroots, he may be safe from a leadership challenge in the near future.Former Green leader Caroline Lucas described the motion as "dangerous" and "flawed from top to bottom", and said leadership "was frankly missing" on it.She said she was not calling for Polanski to stand down and welcomed that he had "indicated he shares some of my concerns on the Zionism motion"."Now the party needs to come together to make the urgent changes needed to take us forward," she said.Jonathan Bartley, the Green co-leader from 2016 to 2021, called on Polanski to "put his hands up" and "say sorry" - but did not demand he quit."I think [the vote] was a failure of leadership from Zack and there is a certain toxicity now around the Green Party," he told BBC Radio 4's World at One.Bartley said the Green brand "needs to be detoxified", adding the party had seen an influx in members that have "maybe come from the left of the Labour Party, maybe from [Jeremy Corbyn's] Your Party" but "we're losing some older voters".The party's next scheduled leadership ballot takes place in summer 2027, and Bartley said he thinks Polanski will face a challenger.Siân Berry, Green MP for Brighton Pavilion, said on Friday she was ready to work with colleagues "to restore trust in our processes and our party, fix the serious flaws in the motion that was passed" and build more inclusive policies.The Green leader has faced days of pressure over the Zionism motion. Four of the five Green MPs and one of the party's two deputy leaders opposed it, the Green deputy in Wales and some councillors resigned, while some local members and the European Green Party have distanced themselves from it.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on Polanski to reverse the "completely wrong" motion.Meanwhile, Labour chair Bridget Phillipson drew comparisons with her party's previous antisemitism scandal, telling the BBC she felt the Greens now face a "serious problem" with antisemitism.Polanski has said anti-Zionism and antisemitism are distinct from each other and said nobody will be excluded from the party on the basis of their faith, place of worship or religious body.

schema.headline: Zack Polanski vows to stay as Green leader as he faces criticism after by-election defeat

title: Lib Dem MP quits frontbench job over Ed Davey's leadership
description: Liberal Democrat MP Charlie Maynard has resigned from the party's frontbench and wants to see Sir Ed Davey replaced as leader.As first reported by the
body: Liberal Democrat MP Charlie Maynard has resigned from the party's frontbench and wants to see Sir Ed Davey replaced as leader.As first reported by the Financial Times, external, the Witney MP left his role as Treasury spokesman on Friday.Those close to Sir Ed privately acknowledge that there is what they see as a "small group" of Liberal Democrat MPs who are not happy with his leadership, of which Maynard is one.Daisy Cooper, the deputy leader of the party, said: "The vast majority of our MPs support Ed, want him to lead the party into the next election, and are furious at this distraction." The BBC has approached Maynard for comment. Lib Dem MP and former leader Tim Farron also defended Sir Ed, saying under his leadership the party was in a position to match or even beat the "record numbers of MPs" the party won at the last election. "To think we're helped by this kind of rubbish, you'd need to be smoking the kind of stuff even we aren't in favour of legalising," he quipped.Several other Lib Dem MPs, including some frontbenchers, also gave Davey their backing in social media posts on Friday evening. Julian Brazil, a Liberal Democrat council leader who has previously been critical of Sir Ed, said Maynard had "put his head above the parapet - we'll see if other people follow".Speaking to BBC Radio 5Live's Matt Chorley, he said: "I would have thought that in the next few days, we will see if there's a groundswell behind him."Brazil added that Sir Ed had been a "fantastic leader" but added: "For whatever reasons people aren't listening to Ed, they don't take notice of him, so we need to have a fresh start and be able to articulate what our vision of the country is."I think that's best done by someone else."Maynard was first elected to his Oxfordshire constituency in 2024, winning the traditionally Conservative seat, formerly held by David Cameron, with a majority of more than 4,000.Before becoming an MP, he ran an international mergers and acquisitions advisory firm. He is the second Lib Dem to leave the frontbench this week, following Alison Bennett's decision to resign her post of spokesperson for care and carers.Bennett would not confirmed why she stepped down but it is understood it was not for personal reasons. Under Liberal Democrat rules, a leadership contest can be triggered if a vote of no confidence in the leader is passed by the majority of all the party's MPs. To enter a leadership contest, a Lib Dem MP must have nominations from at least 10% of the parliamentary party, not including the candidate themselves, and have the backing of 200 members across at least 20 local parties. Sir Ed has been leader for six years and in the 2024 general election led the party to its biggest election success, winning 72 seats. However, the party has found it difficult to build on that success, with polling numbers remaining at relatively low levels. More recently, some Liberal Democrats have publicly attacked the leader for his stance on the triple lock - the mechanism which guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% whichever is highest.Last week, Sir Ed criticised Andy Burnham's announcement that he would adjust the triple lock, arguing it would "put more pensioners into poverty". "This would mean people who are working hard now - the millennials - when they retire would have a very poor pension," he said. One Lib Dem MP described Sir Ed's argument as "nonsense", while another said: "Most millennials don't think there will be a state pension when they retire so this isn't being done with them in mind."

schema.headline: Lib Dem MP quits frontbench job over Ed Davey's leadership

title: Commentator Katie Zacharia picked as new White House press secretary
description: Donald Trump has chosen conservative commentator Katie Zacharia to be the next White House press secretary.Zacharia, who currently works for Trump Med
body: Donald Trump has chosen conservative commentator Katie Zacharia to be the next White House press secretary.Zacharia, who currently works for Trump Media & Technology Group, will become the US president's sixth chief spokesperson across his two administrations. She previously had a brief stint as a spokeswoman at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).Trump called Zacharia "loyal" and "a devoted fan and member of MAGA" in a social media post on Friday, referring to his Make America Great Again movement, adding that she had "an unblemished record of support".Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, who left the White House in August, has reportedly taken a job with Fox News."She was previously involved in my Campaigns, assisting in key Swing States, where we won 7 out of 7," Trump wrote on Truth Social of Zacharia."I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration."Zacharia thanked him in a post on X, writing: "Serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime."She said Trump had "shown America that we can be great again, and he works to effectuate that greatness every single day". She said she looked forward "to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out". The 42-year-old political strategist is a frequent fixture on conservative Newsmax and Fox News, and has been active in Republican politics for most of her adult life, having worked as an intern for the Republican National Committee and for the White House Office of Political Affairs during the Bush administration in 2006.Since June, she has been a senior communications adviser for Trump's media company and Truth Social platform, according to her LinkedIn profile. She worked in Homeland Security from February to March this year.While she was only briefly in government at DHS - which the mother of four later said she left because of the strain of travel between California and Washington on her family - she has long been a ferocious defender of President Trump and his administration's policies.In a June interview with the BBC, for example, she dismissed criticism of Trump's controversial use of the White House to host a televised UFC fight, saying the principles of the UFC "are the kind of principles that founded our Constitutional Republic"."It's about not giving up the fight until the bitter end," she said. "I think there's no better summation of the American ethos than a good UFC fight."Earlier this year, Zacharia wrote an op-ed in the New York Post about an incident in which she was asked to stop wearing a "Make America Great Again" hat to her local gym."I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," she wrote. "This is raw, unfiltered intolerance. Freedom of speech doesn't evaporate at the gym door."Justin Buchler, a political science professor at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio, told the BBC that Trump's appointments during his second term have been "based on personal affiliation and loyalty". "He values loyalty first and foremost," Buchler told the BBC. A lawyer educated at Pepperdine University in California, Zacharia also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally - and current Special Presidential Envoy for Special Missions - Ric Grenell.In 2011, she spent nearly two years clerking at a law firm in Beijing, China.The complex job of press secretary goes beyond the briefing room podium to include managing contentious relationships with the press, coordinating with other parts of the White House, and providing media advice to the president. The secretary also oversees an office that receives a significant amount of inquiries and requests on a daily basis.Yanna Krupnikov, a political scientist and professor of communication and media at the University of Michigan, said the selection of Zacharia "speaks to a blurring of the lines between different media types". Politicians nowadays need to communicate not only to various news outlets but with people in a social media context, she said."I think the goal is not as much speaking to the media and journalists, but making sure that particular, very specific sound-bytes and messages get to ordinary people," Krupnikov told the BBC.When Leavitt left the role, Trump called her one of his "most trusted aides", which sets a high bar for her replacement. Leavitt left because she said she wanted to spend more time with her family.

schema.headline: Commentator Katie Zacharia picked as new White House press secretary

title: Drumcree: Secretary of state Sir Chris Bryant to ban the Drumcree parade
description: Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has said he will ban the contentious Orange Order parade at Drumcree.The dispute has led to a stand-off be
body: Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has said he will ban the contentious Orange Order parade at Drumcree.The dispute has led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks.Sir Chris said the chief constable advised him "it would not be possible to enable the procession to happen without a major intervention which would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect across Northern Ireland".His decision has been welcomed by Sinn Féin and the SDLP, but DUP leader Gavin Robinson said he now needs to "explain what his government intends to do to restore confidence in the rule of law".The move comes on the 13th day of deadlock between residents and the local district lodge of the Orange Order.The Parades Commission had ruled that the march, on Sunday 27 September, could go ahead with restrictions in place.But the parade, from Drumcree Church into Portadown, did not happen due to a large protest on the Garvaghy Road.Under legislation, a secretary of state can overturn a Parades Commission determination, especially following input from the police.Sir Chris had been coming under increasing pressure from Sinn Féin and the SDLP to stop the parade.Chief Constable Jon Boutcher had asked the secretary of state to review the Parades Commission determination allowing the parade.On Friday night, Sir Chris said: "The Parades Commission have advised me that while ultimately a matter for the courts to determine, the commission is of the view that, in light of this current assessment by the chief constable, the original determination does not now have enduring legal effect."Consequently, and in the interests of wider public interest and safety, I've come to the conclusion that the circumstances under which that decision was made have now changed considerably."As a result, the procession cannot go ahead as it was determined."Speaking about Sir Chris' decision, Boutcher said he had outlined to the secretary of state his "current assessment was that all available, lawful and proportionate options to facilitate completion of the procession had been exhausted"."Any remaining options would have required a substantial public order intervention," he said.He added: "Further to this, such an operation would in my view have had not only catastrophic long-term consequences for trust and confidence in policing, but for the Northern Ireland Executive and the peace process."In a statement, the Parades Commission said it "recognises the importance of resolving the issues arising from this dispute and hopes that a way forward can be found through constructive engagement between those concerned".Earlier, First Minister Michelle O'Neill confirmed she had received a letter from police investigating protests over the Drumcree parading dispute.On Thursday, the police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview.There were jubilant scenes at a community hall off Garvaghy Road as the decision over the Drumcree parade was confirmed.Speaking outside the centre, Breandán Mac Cionnaith of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition (GRRC) said that "while this is a win for us tonight, it is one that is still tinged with sadness and with loss"."There's no real cause for celebration that we have to remember the price that was paid to get this decision over many years." One woman was heard saying:  "Best news we've had in years," while another shouted: "No going back."Sinn Féin President Mary Lou McDonald said the overwhelming sense on the road was "one of relief and one of joy", adding that this "awful threat and this sense of menace has been lifted from the community"."To have had the prospect of a march down the road was just incomprehensible, nobody could believe that this decision had been landed and the community said from the get go that they would stand strong and united and that they would not have it and they have. Right has won out here."The Portadown District said the "chief constable has abdicated his responsibility for policing Northern Ireland"."We further note that the secretary of state has bowed to the republican mob, and rewarded criminality. Again, the consequences should be self-evident," they said.They said that they "understand the immense anger which is tonight engulfing our community", but appealed for calm.In a statement on social media, loyalist activist Jamie Bryson said emergency judicial proceedings were being prepared against the secretary of state's decision.Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson said "it has been clear in recent days that due to the actions of Sinn Féin and the total disregard for the recent determination in favour of a parade that the PSNI cannot ensure the safe completion of the parade"."The decision of the chief constable to refer the matter to the secretary of state and his conclusion that the parade cannot proceed is a direct result of republican agitation, mobilisation and the looming threats of potential violence."On Friday night, Orange Order members again walked to police lines at Drumcree, as they have done regularly over the past two weeks, but were halted.There has been stalemate in Portadown since the decision to allow an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road on 27 September.That morning, up to 1,000 people - including politicians such as Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill - blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church a mile to the west.Since then, residents have maintained a constant presence around the road while Orangemen have also repeatedly tried to march the route before being turned back by police.The chief constable said last week that the consequences of police forcing an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road "could be catastrophic".He had said while the PSNI's objective was to facilitate the determination, this could not be done "at all costs".As of last Thursday, the policing operation over the dispute had cost about £3m.Two weeks ago exactly, the Parades Commission issued a determination saying that the Orange Order parade was to be allowed on the Garvaghy Road with restrictions in place. That prompted a legal challenge from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition which opposed the march.The Court of Appeal is considering whether to allow a challenge to the Parades Commission's ruling, which has been lodged by residents. History shows there are no easy options when it comes to the Drumcree parade dispute.Opinions are so deeply divided that any decision is going to cause anger on one side or the other.Portadown Orange Order and their supporters are furious at the latest turn of events.Exactly two weeks ago, it was the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition and their supporters who were enraged, by the original decision on the Drumcree parade.That fury did not turn into violence on the streets.The hope is that the outcome is the same this time.With the Portadown parade dispute causing so much tension in recent weeks, politicians know that there is still a need to keep searching for a lasting solution.At the moment, with feelings running so high, that looks impossible.

schema.headline: Drumcree: Secretary of state Sir Chris Bryant to ban the Drumcree parade

title: JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he won't watch it
description: US Vice-President JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter. Talking with report
body: US Vice-President JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter. Talking with reporters, Vance expressed doubt that the December execution would go forward as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen". He added, that "if it's through live stream, I'm not going to be watching it". Hours later, US President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved the live stream plans but said the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.Hasan killed 13 unarmed US soldiers at a base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32. The firing squad execution would be the first military execution in more than 60 years.The Pentagon announced earlier this week it would execute former US Army major Nidal Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad in the attack on the Fort Hood base. Then on Thursday US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be livestreamed for the public. "People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth explained. Trump, as he left the White House on Friday, was asked about the possibility that visuals of Hasan's execution could be used as propaganda for terrorists. "He killed 13, 14 people, badly wounded 20-some-odd people, and he's totally nuts," Trump said. "So I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."The BBC has contacted the Pentagon for more information about the livestream determination. Speaking to reporters on Friday, Vance condemned Hasan's attack on the base as "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11". Asked about how his Catholic faith impacted his stance on plans to stream a public execution, Vance cast doubt on whether they would happen. But he noted that Hasan, who was a US Army psychiatrist, was meant to treat soldiers for mental illness and other problems and "took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived". The announcement of the livestream plans has been met with criticism from both political parties. Republican Senator John Curtis pointed to Rome's history of a "bloody spectacle" corrupting people who watched them, warning that public executions erode civilisations "when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment".Curtis said that Hegseth's plan "risks feeding that appetite" and urged him to reconsider. "The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent," he said.Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN that the idea was "disgusting" and reminiscent of executions carried out by the Islamic State group.Georgia lawmaker Austin Scott, a Republican, said that he "absolutely" supports the death sentence, but that live-streaming executions "is what jihadists do. America is better than that".The US Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the decision to publicly livestream Hasan's execution, expressing "shock and great sorrow" in a statement.The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming it would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture".All of the platforms have prohibitions in place on violent images and videos, as well as those that show death or glorify or make a spectacle of violence.Meta, owner of Instagram, Facebook and Threads, explicitly bans any live stream of capital punishment. YouTube bans all "violent or gory content intended to shock or disgust viewers".TikTok has a similar rule that bars "extremely graphic, violent, or disturbing content—especially when it could cause viewers emotional distress."   That includes the "moment of someone's death" and "the shooting of an individual".Both YouTube and TikTok make exceptions in instances of "public interest".Asked if a live-stream of an execution qualifies for the exception if it is government-sanctioned , a TikTok spokeswoman said: "Regardless, I'd point you back to the not allowed section which reflects our approach."The policy at X, which has loosened content moderation since billionaire Elon Musk took over the platform, prohibits content "glorifying" of violence. It will remove content depicting when a person dies will be removed if requested by certain parties.Meta, YouTube and X did not respond to multiple BBC requests for comment on whether they would uphold their current policies in the event Hasan's execution is broadcast.

schema.headline: JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he won't watch it

title: Nationwide cashier to repay £12k after stealing from customers
description: A building society cashier who stole thousands of pounds from customers to pay for "lavish" holidays has been ordered to repay more than £12,000.Kelly
body: A building society cashier who stole thousands of pounds from customers to pay for "lavish" holidays has been ordered to repay more than £12,000.Kelly Kershaw, 54, stole £13,333 including from vulnerable and elderly customers at Nationwide in Caernarfon, Gwynedd, even forging the signature of a man with learning disabilities.Kershaw admitted five counts of fraud after colleagues spotted Facebook posts of her on safari in Africa, and on trips to Paris, Tuscany and Dubai.She was jailed for 16 months in May but returned to Caernarfon Crown Court for a Proceeds of Crime Act, external hearing, and told to pay back £12,630.Judge Jones ordered Kershaw to repay the sum within three months or face a further five months in prison.The mother-of-two posted pictures of skiing trips, safaris and romantic European getaways on her Facebook page and boasted she was "living and loving life one adventure at a time."Kershaw's victims included an 85-year-old man who had lost some "cognitive abilities" after suffering a stroke - and she stole £6,300 from him.On one occasion, he came to the branch asking to withdraw £200, but Kershaw logged the withdrawal as £500 and pocketed £300 herself.Another victim was a 49-year-old man with learning difficulties who lost £1,400 to Kershaw - he had his bank card kept in the branch as he was a previous victim of fraud.

schema.headline: Nationwide cashier to repay £12k after stealing from customers

title: US immigration officials defend ICE agents who shot man while his child was in the car
description: US immigration officials have defended the actions of officers who shot and wounded a man in his car in New York on Thursday while his five-year-old s
body: US immigration officials have defended the actions of officers who shot and wounded a man in his car in New York on Thursday while his five-year-old son was in the back seat.Markwayne Mullin, the head of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which runs the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), said officers fired their weapons while trying to arrest a man with a criminal history. "We weren't aware the child was in the car," Mullin said on Friday, arguing that it was the man, Oscar Belgal, who had put his child in danger. Belgal is now being held at a detention facility.The legal organisation representing Belgal told the BBC that lawyers had not yet been able to speak to him. The shooting happened in the residential neighbourhood of Marble Hill.Marcos Charles, a top ICE official, said agents used their vehicles to try and stop Belgal in his car but that he resisted orders to get out and instead accelerated, smashing into two ICE vehicles.Charles said Belgal then "weaponised his vehicle and proceeded to accelerate going towards other officers", adding: "Our officers, using their training, and believing that their life and the life of their partners in the general public were in danger, used their training and fired weapons."The number of officers who fired their weapons is being investigated.Charles said Belgal "was struck by one of the bullets or fragments superficially in the neck". New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who called what happened "unconscionable and incredibly serious", said ICE agents surrounded Belgal's car before opening fire."They wore construction vests and masks that concealed their faces. There is no reasonable way to identify them as ICE agents," Mamdani said. He confirmed the child was unharmed.Mullin said the officers identified themselves and were wearing body-worn cameras that were turned on during the incident. Video of the shooting, including body camera footage, has not been made public but unverified videos on social media appear to align with Mamdani's comments. Body-worn camera footage released by the New York Police Department (NYPD) on Friday shows its officers arriving on scene and attempting to help Belgal after he has been shot. One ICE officer appears to be wearing a neon construction vest and carrying a large gun. The NYPD officers then call for an ambulance and put him in a police car to take him to hospital. They are later seen pulling Belgal from the vehicle and carrying him into the hospital.Mamdani said on Thursday that he had spoken to US President Donald Trump and Mullin for two hours but failed to negotiate Belgal's release. Mamdani said he would ask Trump, who has not yet commented publicly on the shooting, to end ICE enforcement actions in New York. Mullin has said he will not pause enforcement. The DHS said Belgal, 28, was from the Dominican Republic and had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs and weapons possession".Belgal was arrested by police officers in New York in December 2023 and released "a few days later", according to the DHS.New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said there was also still a pending case against Belgal for criminal sale of a controlled substance in 2025. DHS has also alleged Belgal was associated with the Trinitarios, described by the US justice department as a transnational criminal group.Mullin said the DHS believed Belgal "has either indirect or direct knowledge" of a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer shooting, "and that's why he became a target".Mamdani is not the only New York official to have criticised the incident. Governor Kathy Hochul said federal officials needed to provide answers quickly about what happened. "New Yorkers have witnessed far too many acts of violence by a rogue federal agency and untrained agents that operate with impunity," Hochul said, adding that she had spoken to Mullin and Trump as well.There have been several high-profile shootings involving ICE officers this year, including one that caused the death of Renee Good in Minneapolis in January.

schema.headline: US immigration officials defend ICE agents who shot man while his child was in the car

title: Boots has a new owner: Three ways it could affect you
description: Upgrading its portfolio of 1,800 stores is high on the list of Boots' new owners, Wittington Investments. This is the holding company of the Westons -
body: Upgrading its portfolio of 1,800 stores is high on the list of Boots' new owners, Wittington Investments. This is the holding company of the Westons -  a wealthy and retail-steeped Canadian family who used to own Selfridges and currently own several large retailers across the Atlantic.  The UK branch of the family also controls the owner of Primark, Associated British Foods (ABF).What Boots stores might look like in the future has not been disclosed.Business has been good for Boots in recent years, and new-look beauty areas in some of its bigger shops have given shoppers more of a department store experience, according to Sofie Willmott, an associate director and analyst at GlobalData Retail.Since the opening of its first beauty-only store in 2023 in the Battersea Power Station development, it says it has redesigned over 180 beauty halls, while also opening its first fragrance concept store and an Opticians dedicated to luxury eyewear."They should invest in the rest of the chain because they've got such a big store portfolio that I think some of the smaller stores have really lacked investment over time, and I think that is something that they need to kind of catch up with," Willmott says.A more "consistent" look would also be an improvement, Willmott adds. "At the moment there is a bit of a disconnect."Jackie Naghten, a retail industry veteran who has worked for the likes of Top Shop, Marks & Spencer and Debenhams, thinks Boots' stores need to be made "more functional" by not having their health hubs "squeezed in the corner".But Yasmin Trimble, 22, who buys beauty products from Boots, likes how the easy stores are to navigate. "You can get everything you need...it is not confusing. It has got a cleaner aesthetic to it as well."Boots was an early adopter of the loyalty cards commonly offered today by companies offering points and discounts to customers who sign up.Its Advantage card, launched in 1997, is unlikely to go away and remains popular. Naghten doesn't think they would get rid of it. "It's the best-value store card in terms of bang for your buck."The card offers shoppers three points for every pound they spend. Each point is worth 1p.Katie Burrows, 23, is a fan of building up the points to get money off.She mainly shops at Boots for skincare, first aid and medicine, but thinks prices for its sanitary products are "ridiculously expensive" - something her friend Yasmin agrees with.Lewis Harrison believes the loyalty card is also good value, but finds it "frustrating how the rewards points only cover a full transaction"."I wish you could use your points for a partial transaction like you can in Holland and Barrett," the 25-year-old says. "It would be good to use the points towards more expensive transactions."Natalie Berg, retail expert and founder of consultancy NBK Retail, suggests the Advantage card gives Boots "a unique understanding of their customers" and is an asset the new owners "will want to double down on"."As AI and social media change how people discover and buy products, that direct relationship with customers will only become more important."The new owners have already signalled they plan to expand Boots' healthcare service, a booming industry at the moment.The retailer started out as an apothecary, so health is in its roots. Today, it offers a wide range of health and wellbeing services as well as prescriptions and vaccinations through its in-store pharmacies.It also announced earlier this summer it was expanding services for weight loss drugs, which have surged in popularity.Naghten points out that the Weston family's purchase of Boots comes at a time when pharmacies are increasingly going to prescribe more medications and health services, in a bid to ease pressure on GP surgeries and hospitals."They didn't buy this thing for no reason. They have got the blueprint," she says.While health will remain a core part of its business, Boots has other strengths, Naghten adds, in its No7 make-up and skincare products."When you have all these people coming in for health and wellbeing services, they will also be picking up a lipstick," she says.Willmott suggests Boots has an "edge" over its rivals on the health side, given its reputation as an expert.But the company is facing tough competition, which Boots acknowledged affected revenues in its latest financial results. Shoppers, particularly younger ones, are increasingly seeking products online through influencer ads rather than heading to brick-and-mortar shops. There are also other big players, such as Superdrug. And M&S this week announced a new partnership with Sephora, saying it would replace a hundred of its own beauty departments with the brand next year. For 18-year-old Schekina Bourne, Boots is not a "go-to shop" for her. "Even though I can go to Boots even in my area....Superdrug is like closest to me. So, I'll prefer the convenience," she says.Additional reporting by Ben Sturt and Anuk Weerawardana

schema.headline: Boots has a new owner: Three ways it could affect you

title: Screams, haunting scenes and deadly hide-and-seek, as Celebrity Traitors heats up
description: Image caption, Romesh Ranganathan lets out a scream while holding a dead woman's wedding dress in the haunted cabinByPaul GlynnCulture reporterSpoiler
body: Image caption, Romesh Ranganathan lets out a scream while holding a dead woman's wedding dress in the haunted cabinByPaul GlynnCulture reporterSpoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fourth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.Being a Traitor must be a nightmare.While other people are out enjoying their lives, they have to kill it, night after night. Even on the weekend, there is no rest for the wicked.Friday's episode saw the the Traitors at it again, murdering Last of Us actor Bella Ramsey, before the faithfuls did their dirty work for them by banishing another of their own, Julie Hesmondhalgh.The previous episode - watched on Thursday by 10 million people - saw another faithful, unlucky Industry star Myha'la, follow self-sabotaging traitor Richard E Grant out of the castle.And so viewers went into Friday's show knowing that traitors Maya Jama, James Acaster and their newest recruit, Prof Hannah Fry, had been debating murdering one of three Bs: Bella (Ramsey), (James) Blunt and Bash (Sebastian Croft).When Ramsey failed to arrive for breakfast it soon became apparent what wickedness had taken place overnight.Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two playersCelebrity Traitors cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horsesWhere is the Traitors castle, and can you visit it?"That's our biggest threat," explained Jama, in a flashback from the previous night's scenes in the traitors turret. "Get them out the way, that group disperses."Acaster agreed: "People are doubting their instincts after that roundtable. If Bella's proven to be a faithful, they're going to be even more spun out."Jama continued: "Chaos, regardless... Bella, you're a genius, but you gotta go."On receiving the news, Ramsey was shocked but not surprised."I think this is a clever move by the traitors," they responded in the diary room."I was going to re-set and start from the beginning because I got it so wrong with Myha'la."So I think that they were right to murder me because I think I would have maybe figured it out."I guess now we'll never know.Image caption, Bella Ramsey was considered to be the Traitors' "biggest threat" and so had to goBack at breakfast, Hesmondhalgh's apparently earnest but over-the-top reaction to Ramsey's removal immediately raised suspicions.The former Coronation Street star had been voted as the most trustworthy of the group by her peers in episode one and given a shield, but that counted for little by episode four.The cleverest among the group, on paper at least, Fry, found questions being asked of her too as the day rolled on. "I did not choose the traitor life, the traitor life chose me," said the latest recruit to the dark side. "I know there are people who are suspicious of me but I'm going to enjoy every last moment."Comedian and Miss Marple impersonator Miranda Hart is one of them. "Hannah lied to us," she rightly noted, with reference to the professor's confusing shield story that helped to see off Myha'la the night before.Singer and ex-military man James Blunt, however, had other ideas, ramping up his campaign against Hesmondhalgh, whom he believed to be a little too trustworthy to be true.Image caption, The group conversing with the grateful deadFriday's mission raised more money for charity and also raised spirits, but not in a good way.It involved the group paying a visit to a graveside haunted cabin to converse with the dead about matters unresolved."It's creepy, it's giving murder," noted Barbie actress Sharon Rooney on arrival.Comedian Romesh Ranganathan joked that his mum was going to "absolutely hate this", as the the group gathered in a graveside chant led by the booming voice of big dog actor Michael Sheen.The spooky task made Ranganathan himself let out a hellish scream and saw Hart come face-to face with a masked hooded creature, before team-player Croft volunteered to go head-first into a stinky old toilet in scenes resembling ITV's I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here."Guys, it's a little bit of poo," noted hardman Ross Kemp, as all around him gagged. "It's not gonna kill you."Croft received a protective shield for his troubles, at least. "If I'd have put my hands and head down a toilet for nothing, I would've been fuming," he fairly noted.Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in UncloakedImage caption, James Blunt led the charge against faithful Julie Hesmondhalgh and has seemingly now put himself in the frame as a resultThe group, with a little help from the undead, had to find a child's toys and a woman's wedding dress and shoes. This later prompted model Jerry Hall to reminisce about her own wedding to Rolling Stones frontman Mick Jagger."Before I got married to Mick - we'd already been together seven years, had two children - I put on a wedding dress every day until he agreed that we get married," she revealed.Some rancid wine that tasted like "salty bin juice", according to comedian Joanne McNally, topped off possibly the most revolting task yet.On the way back to the castle, YouTuber King Kenny raised more suspicions about Fry having allowed him to grab a shield. "She held off to make herself look a bit innocent," he told his fellow faithfuls.Traitor Jama smartly deflected attention away from herself by latching on to the growing suspicions around Hesmondhalgh.Image caption, Julie Hesmondhalgh bade farewell to her fellow faithfuls, describing the show's reveal as "iconic"Ahead of the roundtable, Fry told producers she knew she would have to fight like her life depended on it - because it did - and try to disguise herself as still being a faithful.Once discussions were under way, she played the sympathy card, claiming she had been left feeling "vulnerable" as she knew her reputation as a brain box would make her a target.Mrs Marple aka Hart wasn't going to let her off the hook that easily, however, noting how Fry's argument the previous night had contradicted that of the innocent but now sadly now departed Myha'la.In a nice moment of levity in another tense debate, comedian Joe Lycett reminded the traitors - and pointedly, Hesmondhalgh - that he would "like to be recruited at some stage". He stressed: "I'm still very much available."Hesmondhalgh laughed about how "going all dry mouthed" while defending herself was not helping her cause. "It would be a cruel move taking the most trusted member of our group," noted Sheen."Cruel but clever," added Hart.Ranganathan offered: "The person that we nominated as our most trustworthy person, we have now completely flipped on."Image caption, Newfound Traitor Hannah Fry survived a stressful episodeThe conclusion was to banish Hesmondhalgh, who, in her parting words, said it had been an "immense experience"."Alas," she continued, confirming her fidelity as tears appeared in eyes around the table: "It may mean I am not a phenomenal actor." Singer Blunt, who had led the charge against her, appears to have now put himself in the frame. He told the group: "I'm so sorry, that's my fault.""He's been wrong about every theory he's came up with," said Rooney."So have I," added a frustrated Croft.Hart declared that "everything is up in the air" now, following Hesmondhalgh's eviction, which King Kenny called the team's "biggest loss" so far.But what of the traitors?First recruit, Acaster's strategy is to continue playing the game as if he is a faithful, he said. Jama is enjoying her time on the dark side while Fry, it's fair to say, is not."You two saved me," Fry told the other two of her stressful day, while back in the turret in their cloaks.The episode ended not with a murder but a fresh twist - the promise of a deathly game of hide-and-seek for four chosen contestants.Image caption, Ross Kemp, Rob Beckett, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and Romesh Ranganathan all looking delighted to have been chosen for a game of killer hide-and-seekThe traitors opted to stay out of the game themselves, before settling on Kemp, Ranganathan, his comic pal Rob Beckett and Little Mix and solo singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock."I think this is gonna mess with everybody's heads," said Fry.Presenter Claudia Winkleman greeted the four of them outside the castle in the dead of night."Have we won?", quipped Ranganathan."If only it was that easy Romesh," replied the host, explaining how when they go down to the woods tonight they'll be in for a big surprise: one of them will be killed face-to-face.Only Pinnock, it was decided, will be immune from murder in the game within a game, though the Traitors aren't to know that.This much terror and mischief and it's not Halloween for weeks yet.Celebrity Traitors continues on Thursday at 20:00 BST on BBC One and iPlayer.Get in touchHave you played a version of the Traitors or another social deduction game at home or socially? Share your experience.

schema.headline: Screams, haunting scenes and deadly hide-and-seek, as Celebrity Traitors heats up

title: Manchester City whistleblower Rui Pinto to remain under witness protection
description: The Portuguese computer hacker who released documents which helped trigger the Premier League investigation into Manchester City will remain in witnes
body: The Portuguese computer hacker who released documents which helped trigger the Premier League investigation into Manchester City will remain in witness protection after authorities in the country suspended the decision to end it. Football Leaks founder Rui Pinto had been scheduled to leave the protection programme on Saturday, a ruling he previously said had put him in a "life-threatening situation".Pinto, 37, disclosed a tranche of confidential football documents, including emails and financial records relating to the English Premier League side.In 2018, he shared documents with German magazine Der Spiegel, which used them for investigations into City's finances and alleged breaches of financial fair play rules.City were recently found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. They have appealed against the decision.Pinto became part of Portugal's witness protection programme in 2020 after agreeing to co-operate with authorities and provide information obtained through the Football Leaks operation.However, in a statement on Friday,, external Portugal's Ministry of Justice said a decision to remove Pinto from witness protection had been reversed for the time being, with the body responsible for it - the special security programmes commission -  having not adequately "notified" Pinto of grounds for its termination or given him the opportunity to challenge the decision. Pinto will now be given 10 days to assess a risk assessment conducted by the special security programmes commission that indicates a low threat to his safety. He posted on X, external thanking Portugal's Minister of Justice, Rita Alarcao Judice and saying the commission's initial decision had clearly violated the law and amounted to a "manifest abuse of power".Pinto has described himself as a whistleblower, but was convicted in Portugal of offences including illegal access to data and attempted extortion and given a four-year suspended sentence.He wore a bulletproof vest during his first trial in 2020, which was also subject to heightened security measures.Earlier this year, he was acquitted of 241 counts of illegally accessing email accounts belonging to a number of sports bodies in Portugal, including Benfica.

schema.headline: Manchester City whistleblower Rui Pinto to remain under witness protection

title: King pays Andrew's £1.5m repair bill on Royal Lodge
description: Mountbatten-Windsor left his Royal Lodge home in February, in the middle of a storm of revelations about his connections to the US sex offender Jeffre
body: Mountbatten-Windsor left his Royal Lodge home in February, in the middle of a storm of revelations about his connections to the US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.He has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.The former Prince Andrew was moved to Sandringham, with his brother the King using his own money to provide his upkeep and accommodation.Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested later that month on suspicion of misconduct in public office - and a court ruling on Thursday found fault with the search warrants used by the police.But despite moving to Sandringham, Mountbatten-Windsor's lease on Royal Lodge had remained until October - and as that officially ends, the Crown Estate is revealing the terms on which it concluded.When Andrew had taken on the 75 year lease in 2003, he had made considerable up-front payments, including about £7.5m for repairs, which meant that he did not have to pay a monthly rent.It also meant that if he gave up the lease within the first 25 years he would be legally entitled to some compensation - with that amount reducing each year.Leaving in October 2026 would have meant that the Crown Estate would have had to pay him back about £302,000.However that amount has been overshadowed by what he owes to the landlord for the state of the building - and so the Crown Estate says it has now received a net amount of £1.5m.It's understood that the payment of that money by the King is to avoid leaving the Crown Estate out of pocket.Whether Mountbatten-Windsor will repay his brother is said to be a private matter - and there are no further details of what this might say about Andrew's personal finances.There was also no comment on how the King feels about this arrangement - and there is said to be no connection between this payment and the King making clear this week that his financial support should not go to cover Andrew's legal costs in his battle over search warrants.It has so far not been decided how the 30-room mansion in Windsor will be used in future, but it is expected to be used to deliver a commercial return - and at present there are no plans for another royal occupant."The lease for Royal Lodge has ended and our focus now is firmly on its future use and the opportunities to generate additional financial value for the nation from its early return," said a Crown Estate spokesperson.A report by the National Audit Office had revealed earlier this year that Mountbatten-Windsor had been sub-letting buildings at Royal Lodge, although the amount was never revealed.That report from the public spending watchdog also showed that Andrew's daughters, Princess Beatrice and Eugenie, had accommodation inside royal palaces which they did not pay for, with the cost being covered privately by the King.

schema.headline: King pays Andrew's £1.5m repair bill on Royal Lodge
